volatile and the Java Memory Model volatile write →read establishes happens-before Other HB edges: unlock→lock (same monitor), Thread.start(), Thread.join(), final-field freeze, executor submit →task start. Happens‐before. Everything Thread A wrote before the volatile write is visible to Thread B after it reads that volatile and sees the new value. Visibility: without a happens‐before edge, another thread may never see a write (CPU caches, JIT hoisting a read out of a loop). Ordering: the compiler and CPU reorder freely within a thread unless HB constraints forbid it. Atomicity: long / double writes are atomic only if volatile ; compound actions are never atomic without locks/CAS. volatile gives visibility + ordering for one variable. Use for flags, published immutable snapshots ( volatile Config current ), double‐checked locking. Safe publication: final fields of a properly constructed object (no this escape) are visible to all threads without synchronization. Deadlocks, Race Conditions, Starvation, Thread Safety Deadlock: circular wait on two locks Prevent: global lock ordering · tryLock(timeout) · fewer, coarser locks · no locks held while calling foreign code/I/O. Detect: jstack / jcmd Thread.print prints "Found one Circular wait. Two threads each hold one lock and wait for the other. All four Coffman conditions — mutual exclusion, hold‐and‐wait, no preemption, circular wait — must hold. Concurrent marking finds live data in Old →mixed GCs. Goal: -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis (default 200 ms). G1 region layout. "What is a TLAB?" — Thread‐Local Allocation Buffer; each thread bumps a pointer in its own Eden chunk, so allocation is extremely cheap. "Stop‐the‐world?" all application threads paused at a safepoint. Even "concurrent" collectors have short STW phases. Saga: Orchestration vs Choreography Orchestrated saga: Place Order — with compensations Order (orchestrator) Payment Inventory Shipping 1 create order PENDING 2 AuthorizePayment PaymentAuthorized 3 ReserveStock StockUnavailable ✗ 4 VoidAuthorization (compensate) 5 order →CANCELLED Happy path continues: StockReserved →CreateShipment →order CONFIRMED. Every step & compensation must be idempotent; state persisted after each step. Orchestrated saga. A coordinator drives each step and issues compensations in reverse order when a step fails. Choreography Orchestration Control each service reacts to others' events central orchestrator sends commands Visibility flow is implicit, spread across services explicit state machine, one place to look Coupling services know each others' events orchestrator knows all participants Good for 2–4 steps, simple flows many steps, branching, timeouts, human steps Tools Kafka + listeners custom state machine, Temporal, Camunda, Axon Risk cyclic event dependencies, hard debugging orchestrator becomes a "god service" SAGA DESIGN RULES Order steps so the least compensable ones come last (charge card after stock reserved; ship last). Compensations are semantic undo (refund, release), not rollbacks; they can fail too →retry until done. Persist saga state after every step; resume after crashes. Give each saga a timeout and a "stuck saga" alert. INTERVIEW QUICK RECALL Sagas give ACD, not I: no isolation. Other transactions may see intermediate states (order PENDING, stock reserved). Countermeasures: semantic locks (status fields), commutative updates, re‐reading values, and versioning. 4.11 Transactional Outbox and Inbox Transactional outbox: atomically change state AND publish an event Order Service @Transactional Guarantee: at-least-once publication (relay may resend after crash) →consumers must be idempotent. CH 5 · DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS The Eight Fallacies and the Failure Model The network is not reliable, latency is not zero, bandwidth is not infinite, the network is not secure, topology does change, there is more than one administrator, transport cost is not zero, the network is not homogeneous. Failure What you observe Key point Crash‐stop node gone simplest to reason about Crash‐recovery node returns with stale/partial state needs durable logs, idempotent replay Omission lost messages retries →duplicates Timing / gray failure node slow but "up" (GC, disk, noisy neighbour) the most common and hardest to detect Byzantine node lies out of scope for typical backends INTERVIEW QUICK RECALL When a request times out you cannot know whether it was not received, processed and the reply was lost, or is still running. Every design decision about retries, idempotency and reconciliation flows from this one fact. 5.2 CAP Theorem and Its Limitations CAP: under a network Partition, a replicated register must choose between Consistency (linearizability) and Availability (every non‐failed node answers). It says nothing when there is no partition. COMMON MISTAKES "Pick two of three" — partitions are not optional, so the real choice is C or A during a partition. Labelling whole databases "CP" or "AP": most systems are configurable per operation (e.g. read/write consistency levels) and many offer neither strict C nor strict A. Equating CAP's "C" with ACID's "C" (constraint validity) — unrelated. PACELC THE MORE USEFUL FRAMING If Partitioned, choose A or C; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. Synchronous replication costs latency on every write even on a healthy network — that's the trade‐off you pay daily. 5.3 Consistency Models Model Guarantee Typical source Linearizable (strong) every op appears to take effect atomically at one instant between call and return; reads see the latest completed write single leader with sync reads, consensus systems (etcd, ZooKeeper), Spanner Sequential all see the same order, consistent with each client's program order (not real time) Causal causally related ops seen in order by all; concurrent ones may differ some geo‐replicated stores, session tokens Read‐your‐ writes a client sees its own writes sticky sessions, read from leader after write Monotonic reads never see older data after newer pin client to one replica Eventual if writes stop, replicas converge async replication, caches, DNS 5.4 Linearizability vs Serializability Linearizability Serializability About single objects/registers, recency multi‐object transactions , isolation Promise ops look instantaneous, real‐time order respected result equals some serial order of transactions (not necessarily real‐time) Context distributed systems, replication databases (ACID "I") Both together strict serializability (e.g. Spanner, FoundationDB)

Replication, Partitioning and Sharding Leader–follower replication and replication lag Anomalies with async lag read-your-writes violated monotonic reads violated (time goes backwards) failover may lose the last ∆t of commits split-brain if old leader keeps accepting writes Leader–follower. Writes go to the leader; followers apply its log. Reading from async followers trades consistency for scale. Approach How Pros Cons Single‐leader one writer, N readers simple, no write conflicts leader is write bottleneck; failover complexity Multi‐leader writes in several regions local write latency conflict resolution required Leaderless (Dynamo‐ style) write/read quorums to any replicas high availability conflicts, read repair, sloppy quorums Partitioning / sharding split data by key range or hash scales writes + storage cross‐shard queries/transactions, rebalancing, hot shards CHOOSING A SHARD KEY High cardinality, evenly distributed, present in almost every query, and aligned with transaction boundaries (e.g. tenant_id , ). Avoid monotonically increasing keys (timestamps, sequences) for hash‐less range sharding — all writes hit the last user_id shard. 5.6 Leader‐Follower Replication and Quorums Quorum reads/writes: N= 3, W= 2, R= 2 →W + R> Nguarantees overlap Read with R = 2 hits {B, C} →at least one replica has v2; pick highest version. Caveats (implementation‐specific): sloppy quorums / hinted handoff break the overlap concurrent writes still need conflict resolution (LWW loses data under clock skew; vector clocks/CRDTs) quorum ≠linearizable without read-repair rules Quorum overlap. With W + R > N, every read quorum intersects every write quorum — necessary but not sufficient for strong consistency. Synchronous follower: commit waits for it →no data loss on failover, higher latency, blocks if the follower is down. Semi‐ sync : wait for one of N. Failover hazards: promoting a lagging follower loses acknowledged writes; old leader comes back and still thinks it's leader (split‐brain) →need fencing (STONITH, epochs, tokens). 5.7 Consensus Basics: Raft and Leader Election Problem: get nodes to agree on a sequence of values despite crashes. Used for leader election, configuration, locks, metadata (etcd →Kubernetes, ZooKeeper, KRaft in Kafka). Raft in four lines: nodes are follower/candidate/leader; a follower that hears no heartbeat becomes candidate, increments the term, requests votes; a majority makes it leader; the leader appends entries and commits once a majority has them. Tolerates ⌊(N−1)/2⌋failures: 3 nodes →1, 5 nodes →2. Even sizes add cost without extra tolerance. Majority requirement means a minority partition cannot make progress (that's the "C" choice). Latency: every commit needs a majority round‐trip; cross‐region clusters pay WAN latency on each write.

"Why not just use a database row as a leader lock?" — you can (with leases and fencing), and it's often fine. The hard part isn't electing a leader; it's ensuring the old leader stops acting — which requires fencing at the resource. 5.8 Distributed Locks, Leases and Fencing Tokens Lease expiry without fencing corrupts data — fencing tokens fix it Client 1 Lock service Client 2 Storage 1 acquire →token 33 long GC pause … lease expires 2 acquire →token 34 3 write(token 34) ✓ 4 write(token 33) →REJECTED (33 < 34) Storage must check tokens (e.g. UPDATE … WHERE fence < :token). A Redis lock alone cannot give this guarantee — the protected resource must participate. The GC‐pause problem. A lease‐based lock holder can't know its lease expired while it was paused. Monotonic fencing tokens let the storage reject stale writers. Never order events across machines by wall‐ clock timestamps for correctness. Measure durations with a monotonic clock ( System.nanoTime() ), not currentTimeMillis() . Lamport clock: counter incremented per event and set to →total order consistent with causality max(local, received)+1 (but can't detect concurrency). Vector clock: one counter per node →detect concurrent updates (conflicts). Hybrid logical clocks (CockroachDB, MongoDB) combine physical time and logical counters. Tail Latency, p95/p99 and Fan‐out Amplification Fan-out amplifies tail latency slow P(request avoids every 1‐in‐100 slow call), n parallel calls: n = 1 →99.0% fast; 1.0% see a p99-slow call n = 10 →90.4% fast; 9.6% see a p99-slow call n = 100 →36.6% fast; 63.4% see a p99-slow call Mitigate: hedged requests, timeouts per shard, partial results, fewer hops. Fan‐out. The more backends a request touches in parallel, the more likely it waits for at least one slow one — your p50 becomes their p99. Report percentiles from histograms , never averages of percentiles (you can't average p99s across pods). Use Prometheus histograms and histogram_quantile . Coordinated omission: load tools that wait for each response before sending the next under‐report tail latency (use open‐ model tools like Gatling/k6 arrival‐rate executors, wrk2). Tail tamers: timeouts, hedged requests (send a 2nd request after p95 delay), fewer sequential hops, avoiding GC pauses, request coalescing. 5.18 Failure Detection and Recovery Heartbeats + timeouts = suspicion , not certainty. Too short →false positives and flapping; too long →slow recovery. Phi‐ accrual detectors adapt to observed variance. Use health checks at several levels: process alive (liveness), can serve (readiness), synthetic end‐to‐end checks. Recovery must be idempotent and resumable: replay from logs/offsets, reconcile, then resume. Producers append records; consumers read at their own pace by offset; records stay for a retention period regardless of consumption. Why it matters: durable decoupling, replay, high throughput, ordered streams per key. Kafka message flow (topic 'orders', 3 partitions, RF = 3, min.insync.replicas = 2) Producer →broker →consumer. The index can seek on any leftmost prefix; a range on one column stops further columns from being used for seeking. AND qty >= 1 — often the best of both 8.11 MVCC Writers create new row versions ; readers see the version visible to their snapshot →readers don't block writers and vice versa. PostgreSQL: old versions stay in the table until VACUUM removes them. Long‐running transactions (or idle‐in‐transaction sessions, abandoned replication slots) prevent cleanup →table/index bloat, and in extreme cases transaction‐ID wraparound protection. MySQL InnoDB: old versions in undo logs; long transactions grow the history list length and slow reads. Monitor: oldest transaction age, n_dead_tup ( pg_stat_user_tables ), autovacuum activity. 8.12 Deadlocks and Lock Contention -- PostgreSQL: who is blocking whom SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by, state, wait_event_type, wait_event, now() - xact_start AS xact_age, left(query, 80) AS query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = current_database() AND state <> 'idle' ORDER BY xact_age DESC; -- MySQL: SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G -- (LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK section) SELECT * FROM performance_schema.data_lock_waits; AVOIDING DEADLOCKS Lock rows in a consistent order (e.g. ascending id) — sort before on many rows. SELECT … FOR UPDATE Keep transactions short; no network calls inside. Index the columns in WHERE of UPDATE / DELETE (unindexed predicates lock far more rows, esp. MySQL gap locks). Set lock_timeout / innodb_lock_wait_timeout and statement_timeout ; retry deadlock victims. 8.13 Connection Pooling and Pool Sizing spring.datasource.hikari: maximum-pool-size: 10 minimum-idle: 10 connection-timeout: 3000 connection (default 30000) max-lifetime: 1680000 timeout leak-detection-threshold: 20000 20 s pool-name: orders-db # per instance — start small # fixed-size pool # ms to wait for a # 28 min SIZING Starting point (PostgreSQL wiki): connections ≈(CPU cores × 2) + effective spindles for the database server , shared by all app instances. Total = pool size × replicas (× HPA max!) must fit under max_connections minus admin headroom. A bigger pool rarely makes a saturated DB faster — it adds contention. Queue in the app, not in the DB. Many services/instances? Put PgBouncer (transaction pooling) in front.

Read Replicas, Replication Lag and Failover Route reads with @Transactional(readOnly = true) + a routing DataSource ( AbstractRoutingDataSource ), or separate repositories per DataSource. Lag makes replicas unsafe for read‐after‐write. Send a user's reads to the primary for a short window after their write, or read from the primary for anything feeding a decision (balances, stock). Monitor lag: PG ; MySQL → pg_stat_replication.replay_lag SHOW REPLICA STATUS Seconds_Behind_Source . Failover: managed services (RDS/Aurora, Cloud SQL) or Patroni / orchestrator. Apps must reconnect: DNS TTLs, max- , retries on connection errors. lifetime 8.15 Partitioning and Sharding -- PostgreSQL declarative partitioning (same server): prune old data cheaply, smaller indexes CREATE TABLE events (id BIGINT, tenant_id BIGINT, occurred_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, payload JSONB) PARTITION BY RANGE (occurred_at); CREATE TABLE events_2026_10 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-10-01') TO ('2026-11-01'); -- drop a month instantly instead of DELETE: DROP TABLE events_2026_04; ⚠destructive Partitioning = split a table inside one DB (pruning, maintenance). Sharding = split data across DB servers (write scale) — needs routing, and makes cross‐shard joins/transactions/unique constraints hard. Queries must include the partition key to benefit from pruning. Shard by tenant or user; keep a directory or consistent‐hash mapping; plan resharding before you need it (Vitess, Citus, app‐level). 8.16 Schema Migrations and Backward‐Compatible Changes EXPAND →MIGRATE →CONTRACT (ZERO DOWNTIME WITH ROLLING DEPLOYS) 2. 3. 4. Expand: add the new column/table (nullable or with default), deploy code that writes both old and new. Migrate: backfill in small batches ( UPDATE … WHERE id BETWEEN … ), throttled. Switch reads to the new column. Contract: stop writing the old column; drop it in a later release. Operation PostgreSQL MySQL 8 Add nullable column / with constant default instant (PG 11+) ALGORITHM=INSTANT Create index without blocking writes (not inside a TX; check for CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY INVALID on failure) online DDL ( ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE ) Add NOT NULL to existing column add CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID → VALIDATE CONSTRAINT → SET NOT NULL table rebuild; use gh‐ost/pt‐osc for big tables Rename column breaks old code →expand/contract instead same Long‐running DDL waiting for a lock blocks everything queued behind it →set lock_timeout lock_wait_timeout Tools: Flyway or Liquibase, versioned and run once per deploy (or as a K8s Job), never ddl-auto: update in production. 8.17 Transactions Across Services There is no practical distributed ACID across microservices; 2PC/XA is fragile (blocking coordinator, poor support in modern brokers). Use: Saga with compensations (Chapter 4) for business workflows. Outbox for "change DB + publish event" atomically. Idempotent consumers + reconciliation jobs to repair drift. Re‐draw boundaries if two services constantly need atomic updates together.

CH 9 · DOCKER Images vs Containers; Layers and Caching Image Container What immutable, layered filesystem + metadata (entrypoint, env, user) a running (or stopped) instance: image + writable layer + namespaces/cgroups Identity content digest sha256:… (tags are movable pointers) container ID Lifecycle build →push →pull create →start →stop →rm Each RUN , COPY , ADD creates a layer. The build cache is reused until the first changed instruction; everything after is rebuilt. Order instructions from least to most frequently changing: base →OS packages →dependency manifest →dependencies →source code. Deleting files in a later layer does not shrink the image (they still exist in the earlier layer). Clean up in the same RUN . 9.2 Multi‐stage Build for Spring Boot (Production‐oriented) Multi-stage build + layered Spring Boot JAR →small, cache-friendly image Layers are cached top-down: put rarely-changing content first so a code change re-uploads only a few hundred KB. Two stages. Build with a full JDK and Maven cache; ship only a JRE plus the extracted application layers. RUN groupadd --system --gid 10001 app && useradd --system --uid 10001 --gid app --no-create-home app WORKDIR /app COPY --from=build --chown=app:app /workspace/extracted/dependencies/ COPY --from=build --chown=app:app /workspace/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ COPY --from=build --chown=app:app /workspace/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./ COPY --from=build --chown=app:app /workspace/extracted/application/ USER 10001:10001 EXPOSE 8080 ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError - XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp" # exec form →java is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"] ./ ./ ./

MaxRAMPercentage CPU: always set requests (used for scheduling and HPA %). LimitRange Use a namespace for defaults and ResourceQuota for team caps. 10.5 Liveness vs Readiness vs Startup Probes Probe timeline: startup →readiness / liveness startupProbe running liveness + readiness probes active JVM start, Flyway, cache warm-up. Liveness/readiness paused until it passes. readiness fails pod removed from Service endpoints — no traffic, NOT restarted liveness fails kubelet kills & restarts the container (restart count ↑) startup fails after failureThreshold × periodSeconds →container restarted Rule: liveness = 'is this process wedged?' (local only). Readiness = 'can I serve right now?'. Never put shared dependencies in liveness. Three probes, three consequences. Readiness controls traffic, liveness controls restarts, startup protects slow boots. Startup Liveness Readiness Question has the app finished starting? is the process irrecoverably stuck? can it serve traffic right now? On failure restart (after threshold) restart container remove from Service endpoints, keep running Should check same as liveness in‐process state only (event loop alive, no deadlock) own readiness; optionally critical local deps Must not check — DB, Redis, downstream services other services' health (cascades) Spring Boot /actuator/health/ liveness /actuator/health/liveness /actuator/health/readiness

Liveness = readiness = /actuator/health (which includes DB) →DB blip restarts every pod at once. • on liveness instead of a startup probe →slow detection forever. initialDelaySeconds: 120 timeoutSeconds: 2–3 Probe timeout (default 1 s) shorter than GC pauses under load →false restarts. Use . 10.6 Horizontal Pod Autoscaler apiVersion: autoscaling/v2 kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler metadata: { name: orders } spec: scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: orders } minReplicas: 3 maxReplicas: 12 metrics: - type: Resource resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 65 } } behavior: scaleUp: scaleDown: { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300, policies: [ { type: Pods, # × DB pool size must fit DB max_connections! # % of REQUEST { value: 1, stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0, periodSeconds:60}]} policies: [ { type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds:60}]} Needs metrics‐server (CPU/memory) or a custom/external metrics adapter (Prometheus Adapter, KEDA for Kafka lag / queue depth). Memory‐based HPA works poorly for JVMs (heap rarely shrinks). 10.7 Rolling Updates and Rollbacks Command Purpose kubectl set image deploy/orders app=registry.example.com/orders:1.14.3 trigger a rollout (prefer GitOps/Helm in practice) kubectl rollout status deploy/orders --timeout=5m wait for success (CI gate) kubectl rollout history deploy/orders revisions kubectl rollout undo deploy/orders --to-revision=7 roll back to a previous ReplicaSet kubectl rollout restart deploy/orders restart pods gradually (e.g. pick up a new Secret) kubectl rollout pause/resume deploy/orders batch several changes into one rollout Progressive delivery (canary, blue‐green, automated analysis) →Argo Rollouts or Flagger. CH 11 · SYSTEM DESIGN — HLD AND LLD The Method: Requirements, Constraints and Flow System design interview flow (45–60 min) A repeatable interview / design‐review flow. Spend the first 10 minutes on steps 1–4; most weak designs fail there, not in the boxes. FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS Who are the users/actors? Core use‐cases (3–5 max). Out of scope? Read vs write paths; sync vs async expectations. Must‐have invariants ("a seat is never sold twice", "money is never lost"). NON‐FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS Scale: DAU, peak QPS, data size/growth, read:write ratio. Latency targets (p99), availability SLO, durability (RPO/RTO). Consistency per operation; geo/regulatory constraints; cost. Security & privacy; operability (who runs it at 3 a.m.?). 11.2 Capacity Estimation and Back‐of‐the‐Envelope Maths Shortcut Value Seconds per day 86,400 ≈10⁵ 1 M requests/day ≈12 QPS average 100 M DAU × 10 req/day 10⁹/10⁵ = 10⁴ QPS avg →plan peak ≈2–5× Storage items/day × size × retention × replication factor (×3) Bandwidth QPS × payload size (10⁴ × 10 KB = 100 MB/s) Cache size 20% of daily hot items × size (80/20 rule) Servers peak QPS ÷ sustainable QPS per instance (measure; don't guess) + N+1 / zone redundancy Latency (orders of magnitude; hardware-dependent) L1 / RAM reference ~1 ns / ~100 ns Read 1 MB sequentially from RAM ~10s of μs SSD random read ~10s–100 μs Round trip within a datacenter / AZ ~0.1–0.5 ms Redis GET over the network ~0.2–1 ms Indexed DB query (warm) ~1–5 ms Cross‐region round trip ~50–150 ms INTERVIEW QUICK RECALL State assumptions out loud, round aggressively, and use the numbers to make a decision ("10 TB/year →single Postgres is fine for 3 years with partitioning") — estimates that don't change the design are wasted time. 11.3 API Design and Database Schema Design APIs: resource‐oriented, versioned, idempotent writes ( Idempotency-Key ), cursor pagination, clear error model (ProblemDetail). Define request/response for the 3–5 core use‐cases. Schema: start from access patterns →pick primary keys and indexes for them; decide what must be transactional together (aggregate); define partition/shard key early if scale demands it. Write the sequence for the most critical flow (who calls whom, sync/async, where state is persisted, what happens on failure).

Building Blocks: Load Balancing, Caching, Queues, Storage Need Building block Watch out for Spread traffic L4/L7 load balancer, DNS, anycast/CDN sticky sessions (avoid), health checks, connection draining Reduce read latency/load CDN, Redis, in‐process cache invalidation, stampede, consistency Decouple / absorb spikes Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ ordering, duplicates, DLQ, lag Relational data + transactions PostgreSQL/MySQL (+ replicas, partitioning) write scaling, connection limits Massive key‐based writes Cassandra, DynamoDB query‐first modelling, no joins Search / free text / facets Elasticsearch/OpenSearch eventual consistency with source of truth Blobs / files object storage (S3/GCS) + CDN pre‐signed URLs, lifecycle policies Time‐series metrics Prometheus/Mimir, TimescaleDB cardinality Coordination etcd, ZooKeeper, DB leases fencing 11.5 Consistency, Availability, Fault Tolerance and DR Concern Typical decision Consistency vs availability strong for money/inventory/auth; eventual for feeds, counts, search, analytics Single‐AZ failure ≥3 replicas across AZs; DB with synchronous standby in another AZ Region failure active‐passive with async replication (RPO > 0) or active‐active with conflict strategy (costly) Dependency failure timeouts, circuit breakers, graceful degradation, queues for retry Data loss backups + tested restores , point‐in‐time recovery, immutable/offsite copies Bad deploy canary, feature flags, fast rollback, backward‐compatible schemas Security & observability by default: authN at edge + service identity inside, encryption in transit/at rest, least privilege, audit logs; RED metrics per endpoint, traces across hops, SLO‐based alerts. Cost & operational complexity: every extra datastore is a new on‐call skill — justify it. 11.6 Reference Design 1 — URL Shortener URL shortener Client Reads ≫writes (100:1) →cache + CDN at the edge. Click analytics async via Kafka, never on the redirect path. URL shortener. Read‐heavy key lookup with cache and edge caching. Aspect Design notes Key APIs POST /urls {longUrl, customAlias?, expiresAt?} →{code} · GET /{code} →301/302 Location Data model urls(code PK, long_url, owner_id, created_at, expires_at) ; index owner_id Code generation counter ranges per node (ZK/DB‐allocated blocks) →base62 (7 chars ≈3.5 × 10¹² codes); or random + uniqueness check; avoid hashing long URL (collisions, same URL →same code) Flow redirect: CDN →Redis →DB on miss →populate; analytics event to Kafka asynchronously Bottlenecks redirect QPS, hot links →CDN caching (302 if you need every click counted, 301 caches in browsers) Failure modes ID allocator down →nodes keep using pre‐allocated ranges; cache down →DB read replicas Scaling KV store or sharded SQL by code ; read replicas; TTL purge job Trade‐offs sequential codes are guessable (privacy) vs random codes need collision checks

Reference Design 2 — Rate Limiter Distributed rate limiter Clients Local in-memory pre-check for very hot keys; fail-open vs fail-closed is a product decision; sync rules, not per-request lookups. Rules per plan (config svc) Rate limiter. Atomic counters in Redis keyed by client + route, enforced at the gateway. Aspect Design notes Key APIs internal: allow(key, cost) →{allowed, remaining, retryAfter} ; HTTP: 429 + Retry-After , RateLimit-* headers Data model Redis hash per key {tokens, ts} with TTL; rules config (plan, route) →(rate, burst) Algorithm token bucket (bursts OK) or sliding‐window counter (smooth); fixed window only for coarse limits Bottlenecks Redis round‐trip per request; hot keys (one big tenant) Failure modes Redis down →fail‐open (availability) or fail‐closed (protection); local fallback limiter Scaling Redis Cluster with hash tags; local token pre‐allocation (batch 10 tokens) to cut round‐trips Trade‐offs precision vs latency/cost; global vs per‐region limits (per‐region is simpler, slightly over‐admits) 11.8 Reference Design 3 — Notification Service Notification service Producers order, payment… retry w/ backoff →DLT; rate-limit per provider; status log Notification service. Accept fast, deliver asynchronously per channel with retries and provider isolation. Aspect Design notes Key APIs POST /notifications {userId, template, params, channels?, dedupKey, priority} →202; GET / notifications/{id} status Data model notifications(id, user_id, template, status, channel, attempts, dedup_key UNIQUE) ; user preferences & quiet hours; templates (versioned, localized) Flow validate →dedup →resolve prefs →render →enqueue per channel →worker sends →status callbacks (delivery receipts) Bottlenecks provider rate limits, bursts (marketing campaigns) →separate priority topics so OTPs aren't stuck behind promos Failure modes provider outage →circuit breaker + secondary provider; retries with backoff →DLT; duplicate sends →dedup key Scaling partition topics by user; scale workers per channel independently Trade‐offs at‐least‐once delivery (rare duplicate) vs at‐most‐once (rare loss): OTP vs marketing differ

Reference Design 4 — Ticket Booking Ticket booking — hold seats, then pay User Waiting room virtual queue Confirm = UPDATE seats SET status='BOOKED' WHERE id IN (…) AND status='HELD' AND hold_id=:h →rows must match, else fail. Expired holds release seats. Ticket booking. Temporary holds with expiry, final confirmation guarded by the database. Aspect Design notes Key APIs GET /shows/{id}/seats · POST /holds {showId, seatIds} →holdId, expiresAt · POST /bookings {holdId, paymentToken} Data model seats(show_id, seat_id, status AVAILABLE/HELD/BOOKED, hold_id, hold_expires_at, version) , PK (show_id, seat_id) ; bookings , payments Invariant no double booking →enforced by DB conditional update / unique constraint, not by cache Flow hold (conditional UPDATE where AVAILABLE, or Redis SET NX per seat + DB) →pay with idempotency key → confirm (UPDATE where HELD and hold matches) →release on expiry/failure Bottlenecks flash sales: 100× traffic on one show →virtual waiting room, rate limits, cache seat map (stale OK for display) Failure modes payment succeeds but confirm fails →reconcile from PSP webhook, refund if seat gone; hold expiry sweeper Trade‐offs pessimistic locks (simple, contention) vs optimistic conditional updates (scales, retries) 11.10 Reference Design 5 — Distributed Job Scheduler Distributed job scheduler Job API create/cancel Claim: UPDATE jobs SET lease_until = now() + interval '60 s', owner = :me WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE next_run_at Results history Job scheduler. Leases + SKIP LOCKED let many schedulers claim due jobs without double execution in the normal case. Aspect Design notes Key APIs POST /jobs {type, payload, schedule (cron/at), timeout, retries} · DELETE /jobs/{id} · GET /jobs/ {id}/runs Data model jobs(id, cron, next_run_at, status, lease_until, owner, attempts) ; job_runs(job_id, started_at, finished_at, result) Flow schedulers poll due jobs with lease →enqueue →workers execute with heartbeat →record run →compute next_run_at Bottlenecks polling hot index next_run_at ; thundering herd at :00 →jitter schedules Failure modes worker dies →lease expires →re‐run (so jobs must be idempotent); clock skew →use DB now() Scaling partition jobs by hash(id) across scheduler shards; time‐bucketed tables / delay queues for huge volumes Trade‐offs exactly‐once impossible →at‐least‐once + idempotency; simplicity (DB) vs throughput (dedicated queue)

Reference Design 6 — Ride Booking Drivers GPS every 4 s Riders Offer ride to one driver at a time with timeout (driver lock with TTL) →avoid double assignment. Shard geo index by city/region. Ride booking. High‐frequency location writes go to an in‐memory geo index; trips are durable state machines. Aspect Design notes Key APIs PUT /drivers/{id}/location (stream) · POST /rides {pickup, dropoff} · POST /rides/{id}/accept · WebSocket updates Data model ephemeral: driver location + status in geo index (geohash/H3 cell →drivers); durable: trips(id, rider, driver, state, fare, timestamps) Flow rider requests →matching queries nearby available drivers →offer to best driver with TTL lock →accept →trip state machine REQUESTED→ACCEPTED→ARRIVED→IN_PROGRESS→COMPLETED Bottlenecks location write rate (drivers × 1/4 s) →in‐memory, sharded by region; don't write each ping to SQL Failure modes driver accepts two rides →atomic driver status transition; phone offline →timeouts & reassignment Trade‐offs matching quality (global optimisation) vs latency (greedy nearest) 11.12 Reference Design 7 — News Feed News feed — hybrid fan-out Kafka PostCreated Push (fan-out on write) for normal users; pull (fan-out on read) for accounts with millions of followers. Celebrity posts pull at read News feed. Precompute feeds for most users; merge celebrity posts at read time. Aspect Design notes Key APIs POST /posts · GET /feed?cursor=… · POST /follow/{id} Data model ; follow graph ; feed cache: ZSET posts(id, author_id, created_at, …) (follower, followee) feed:{user} of post ids scored by time/rank Flow write: store post →event →fan‐out workers push id into followers' feeds (skip inactive users). Read: get ids from feed cache, merge pulled celebrity posts, hydrate posts (batch cache), rank Bottlenecks fan‐out to millions of followers (celebrity problem) →pull model for them; hydration N+1 →multi‐get Failure modes fan‐out lag →feed slightly stale (acceptable); cache loss →rebuild from graph + posts Trade‐offs push = fast reads, expensive writes; pull = cheap writes, slow reads; hybrid = complexity

Reference Design 8 — File Storage Service dedup by hash delta sync: upload changed chunks only conflict: keep both versions File storage. Metadata in a database, content‐addressed chunks in object storage, devices sync via a change feed. Aspect Design notes Key APIs POST /files/{path}/uploads →presigned chunk URLs · POST /files/{path}/commit {chunkHashes, baseVersion} ·GET /changes?cursor= files(id, owner, path, latest_version) ;file_versions(file_id, version, chunk_list, size, Data model created_at) ; chunks in object store keyed by hash Flow client chunks + hashes →asks which chunks are missing →uploads only those →commits version (optimistic on baseVersion ) →change feed notifies other devices Bottlenecks metadata DB hot for big shared folders; large uploads →resumable multipart Failure modes partial upload →commit is atomic, orphan chunks garbage‐collected; conflict →keep both copies Trade‐offs dedup saves storage but complicates deletion/encryption (per‐user keys break cross‐user dedup) 11.14 Reference Design 9 — E‐commerce Order and Payment E-commerce order & payment workflow Client Order svc Payment svc PSP Inventory 1 POST /orders (Idempotency-Key) 2 reserve stock (TTL) order PENDING_PAYMENT + outbox 201 {orderId, payUrl} 3 pay (key = orderId) authorize/capture 4 webhook: succeeded (verify sig) PaymentSucceeded (Kafka) 5 commit reservation Webhooks arrive late, twice or out of order →dedup by PSP event id; nightly reconciliation against PSP reports. Order + payment. Reserve, pay with idempotency, confirm via events; webhooks and reconciliation close the loop. Aspect Design notes Key APIs POST /orders (Idempotency‐Key) · POST /payments {orderId} · PSP webhook POST /psp/webhooks · GET / orders/{id} orders(id, customer, status, total, version) ,order_lines ;payments(id, order_id UNIQUE, psp_ref, Data model status, amount) ; outbox ; inventory reservations(order_id, sku, qty, expires_at) Flow create order PENDING + reserve stock (TTL) →pay →webhook → order PAID →fulfilment. Failure/timeout →release stock, cancel order (saga) →confirm reservation → PaymentSucceeded Bottlenecks inventory hot SKUs (flash sale) →atomic conditional decrement, per‐SKU queues Failure modes duplicate webhooks, lost webhooks (poll PSP), payment captured but order cancelled →automatic refund; reconciliation daily

OAuth 2.0 OpenID Connect (OIDC) JWT What authorization framework: delegated access via access tokens authentication layer on OAuth 2.0: who the user is a token format (signed JSON claims) Gives you access token (+ refresh token) ID token (always a JWT) + / userinfo — Audience resource servers (APIs) the client application anyone who validates it Flows auth code + PKCE (users), client credentials (services), device code auth code + PKCE used by both; access tokens may also be opaque TOKEN HANDLING Validate: signature via JWKS (cache, handle key rotation), / (small clock skew), allow‐list. iss , aud , exp nbf alg Short‐lived access tokens (5–15 min); refresh tokens rotated, bound to client, revocable. Automate certs (cert‐ manager, ACME); alert well before expiry. mTLS: both sides present certificates →strong service identity; typically delivered by a service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) with SPIFFE IDs, so apps don't manage certs. AFTER: BLAMELESS POSTMORTEM Timeline, impact, detection time, mitigation time. Contributing factors (rarely one "root cause"): technical + process. What went well / what was lucky. Pauses, clock drift, failover; need leases plus fencing tokens. What delivery guarantee do you design for? At‐least‐once + idempotency. What causes cascading failures? Saturated threads/connections propagating upstream, retry storms, restart storms. What is backpressure? Slowing producers when consumers can't keep up — bounded queues, pull‐based consumption. How do you handle hot keys/partitions? Better keys, salting, local caches, splitting tenants. What is consistent hashing? Ring mapping keys to the next node; minimal movement on resize; virtual nodes for balance. SLI vs SLO vs SLA? Measurement vs internal target vs contractual promise.
